summary.text: Direct evaluation supplies a witness at each proposed minimum and exhausts all smaller moduli for the first five cases. For the last case, the proof observes that any admissible divisor \(d\mid m\) must be unitary: cancelling \(d\) gives \(d^{d-1}\equiv1\pmod{m/d}\), forcing \(\gcd(d,m/d)=1\); a finite square-root divisor count then eliminates moduli with fewer than ten unitary divisors, and direct modular computation excludes the remaining moduli below the candidate.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(k)=\#\{d:d\mid k\text{ and }d^d\equiv d\pmod k\}.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(r)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N:F(k)=r\}.
\]
(If the search is taken over positive integers instead, nothing changes below. With the convention used here, the divisor set of \(0\) is empty, so \(F(0)=0\).)

We shall prove that
\[
a(1)=1,
\quad a(2)=2,
\quad a(3)=6,
\quad a(6)=30,
\quad a(7)=210,
\quad a(10)=2310.
\]
The first five minimality assertions require only short finite enumerations. For the last one, we first establish a useful sieve that drastically reduces the finite computation.

### 1. A necessary condition on a counted divisor

Call a divisor \(d\mid k\) a *unitary divisor* of \(k\) if
\[
\gcd(d,k/d)=1.
\]
We claim that every divisor counted by \(F(k)\) is unitary.

Indeed, suppose that \(d\mid k\) and
\[
d^d\equiv d\pmod k.
\]
Write \(k=dq\). If \(d=1\), then \(\gcd(d,q)=1\) immediately. Now suppose \(d>1\). Since
\[
d^d-d=d\bigl(d^{d-1}-1\bigr)
\]
and \(dq\mid d(d^{d-1}-1)\), cancellation of the positive factor \(d\) gives
\[
q\mid d^{d-1}-1,
\]
or equivalently
\[
d^{d-1}\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
If \(g\) divides both \(d\) and \(q\), then \(g\mid d^{d-1}\), because \(d-1\geq1\), while the displayed congruence implies that \(g\mid d^{d-1}-1\). Hence \(g\mid1\), so \(g=1\). Therefore \(\gcd(d,q)=1\), proving the claim.

Let
\[
U(k)=\#\{d:d\mid k\text{ and }\gcd(d,k/d)=1\}
\]
be the number of unitary divisors. The claim gives the fundamental bound
\[
F(k)\leq U(k). \tag{1}
\]

There is a particularly simple finite procedure for computing \(U(k)\). Run through the integers \(d\geq1\) for which \(d^2\leq k\). If \(d\mid k\) and \(\gcd(d,k/d)=1\), add two to the count, except that one adds only one when \(d^2=k\). This is correct because the divisors of \(k\) occur in pairs \(d,k/d\), exactly one member of each nonsquare pair is at most \(\sqrt k\), and
\[
\gcd(d,k/d)=\gcd(k/d,d),
\]
so either both members of a pair are unitary or neither is. In particular, this square-root enumeration computes exactly \(U(k)\).

### 2. The finite computations

For completeness, we describe exactly how all modular entries in the computations below were obtained. For a modulus \(m>0\), define a running modular-power calculation by
\[
R_m(b,0,c)=c\bmod m,
\]
\[
R_m(b,e+1,c)=R_m\bigl(b,e,(cb)\bmod m\bigr).
\]
An induction on \(e\) gives
\[
R_m(b,e,c)\equiv cb^e\pmod m,
\quad 0\leq R_m(b,e,c)<m,
\]
so in particular \(R_m(b,e,1)=b^e\bmod m\). Thus, for each \(k\), one may run through \(d=1,2,\ldots,k\), retain \(d\) if \(k\bmod d=0\), and then retain it a second time precisely when
\[
R_k(d,d,1)=d\bmod k.
\]
The number finally retained is exactly \(F(k)\). This uses only division with remainder, multiplication, and comparison, and supplies a direct reproducible enumeration of every finite range used below.

Applying this enumeration at the six proposed least values gives the following complete lists of successful divisors:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
k&\{d\mid k:d^d\equiv d\pmod k\}&F(k)\\ \hline
1&1&1\\
2&1,2&2\\
6&1,3,6&3\\
30&1,5,6,10,15,30&6\\
210&1,15,21,35,70,105,210&7\\
2310&1,21,55,77,210,231,330,385,1155,2310&10
\end{array} \tag{2}
\]
Here each row is obtained by listing all divisors of the number in the first column and applying the modular-power recurrence above; thus the displayed lists also assert that every omitted divisor fails the congruence. In particular, (2) proves that each proposed value belongs to the appropriate set whose minimum defines \(a(r)\).

We next rule out all smaller values. Direct enumeration in the five short initial ranges produces the following frequency table. The row headed \(0\leq k<B\) gives, for each possible value \(j\), the number of integers \(k\) in that range for which \(F(k)=j\); unlisted frequencies are zero.
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
B&\#\{k:0\leq k<B,\ F(k)=j\}\text{, written as }j:\#\\ \hline
1&0:1\\
2&0:1,\ 1:1\\
6&0:1,\ 1:1,\ 2:4\\
30&0:1,\ 1:1,\ 2:16,\ 3:10,\ 4:2\\
210&0:1,\ 1:1,\ 2:73,\ 3:94,\ 4:24,\ 5:13,\ 6:4
\end{array} \tag{3}
\]
The frequencies in every row sum to \(B\), so every integer in the indicated interval is accounted for. The same direct procedure described above computes each entry: test all \(d=1,\ldots,k\) for divisibility and then evaluate \(d^d\bmod k\) by the recurrence \(R\).

The first row of (3) shows that no \(k<1\) has \(F(k)=1\). The second shows that no \(k<2\) has \(F(k)=2\). The third has no value \(3\), the fourth no value \(6\), and the fifth no value \(7\). Combined with (2), these respectively prove
\[
a(1)=1,
\quad a(2)=2,
\quad a(3)=6,
\quad a(6)=30,
\quad a(7)=210. \tag{4}
\]

It remains to establish the larger minimality assertion \(a(10)=2310\). For every \(k<2310\), first compute \(U(k)\) by the square-root divisor-pair procedure. If \(U(k)<10\), inequality (1) immediately gives \(F(k)<10\), so such a \(k\) cannot contribute. There are only 101 survivors with \(U(k)\geq10\). For those survivors, compute \(F(k)\) by the direct modular procedure. The complete results, grouped into intervals of length 100, are as follows. In the third column, an entry \(j:c\) means that exactly \(c\) of the candidates in that block have \(F(k)=j\).
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|l}
\text{range for }k&\#\{k:U(k)\geq10\}&\text{frequencies of }F(k)\text{ on those candidates}\\ \hline
0\text{--}99&0&\\
100\text{--}199&0&\\
200\text{--}299&1&7:1\\
300\text{--}399&2&7:1,\ 8:1\\
400\text{--}499&2&6:1,\ 7:1\\
500\text{--}599&3&6:1,\ 7:2\\
600\text{--}699&3&6:2,\ 7:1\\
700\text{--}799&4&5:1,\ 6:1,\ 7:1,\ 8:1\\
800\text{--}899&3&6:1,\ 8:2\\
900\text{--}999&5&5:1,\ 6:2,\ 7:1,\ 8:1\\
1000\text{--}1099&3&6:1,\ 7:2\\
1100\text{--}1199&6&6:2,\ 7:3,\ 8:1\\
1200\text{--}1299&5&5:2,\ 6:2,\ 7:1\\
1300\text{--}1399&7&5:1,\ 6:1,\ 7:4,\ 9:1\\
1400\text{--}1499&5&5:1,\ 6:2,\ 7:2\\
1500\text{--}1599&7&5:2,\ 6:1,\ 7:1,\ 8:1,\ 9:2\\
1600\text{--}1699&4&5:1,\ 7:3\\
1700\text{--}1799&7&4:1,\ 6:4,\ 8:1,\ 9:1\\
1800\text{--}1899&7&3:1,\ 4:1,\ 6:3,\ 7:2\\
1900\text{--}1999&7&5:4,\ 6:1,\ 7:1,\ 9:1\\
2000\text{--}2099&7&5:1,\ 6:4,\ 7:1,\ 8:1\\
2100\text{--}2199&7&5:1,\ 6:2,\ 7:3,\ 8:1\\
2200\text{--}2299&6&6:3,\ 7:1,\ 8:2\\
2300\text{--}2309&0&
\end{array} \tag{5}
\]
For additional clarity about the exhaustiveness of the sieve, the 101 candidates represented in (5) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&210,330,390,420,462,510,546,570,630,660,690,714,770,780,798,840,858,870,\\
&910,924,930,966,990,1020,1050,1092,1110,1122,1140,1155,1170,1190,1218,1230,\\
&1254,1260,1290,1302,1320,1326,1330,1365,1380,1386,1410,1428,1430,1470,1482,\\
&1518,1530,1540,1554,1560,1590,1596,1610,1638,1650,1680,1710,1716,1722,1740,\\
&1770,1785,1794,1806,1820,1830,1848,1860,1870,1890,1914,1932,1938,1950,1974,\\
&1980,1995,2002,2010,2030,2040,2046,2070,2090,2100,2130,2142,2145,2170,2184,\\
&2190,2210,2220,2226,2244,2262,2280.
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
To reproduce (6), for each \(1\leq k<2310\) run over \(d\leq\sqrt k\), pair \(d\) with \(k/d\), and count precisely the pairs satisfying \(d\mid k\) and \(\gcd(d,k/d)=1\), as justified above. Retain exactly those totals at least ten. Then the modular recurrence \(R_k(d,d,1)\), applied to every divisor of each retained \(k\), gives (5). As checks on completeness, the candidate counts in the second column of (5) sum to 101, and the overall frequency distribution in the final computation is
\[
F=3:1,
\quad 4:2,
\quad 5:15,
\quad 6:34,
\quad 7:32,
\quad 8:12,
\quad 9:5,
\]
whose frequencies also sum to 101.

Now let \(k<2310\). If \(U(k)<10\), then \(F(k)<10\) by (1). If \(U(k)\geq10\), then \(k\) is one of the candidates in (6), and (5) shows that \(3\leq F(k)\leq9\). Thus in all cases
\[
F(k)\ne10.
\]
On the other hand, the last row of (2) gives \(F(2310)=10\). Therefore
\[
a(10)=2310. \tag{7}
\]

### 3. Identification with the primorials

Let \(p_n\#\) denote the product of the first \(n\) primes, with the empty product equal to \(1\). The first five primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
A002110(0)&=1,\\
A002110(1)&=2,\\
A002110(2)&=2\cdot3=6,\\
A002110(3)&=2\cdot3\cdot5=30,\\
A002110(4)&=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210,\\
A002110(5)&=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining these identities with (4) and (7) yields exactly
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
a(1)&=A002110(0)=1,\\
a(2)&=A002110(1)=2,\\
a(3)&=A002110(2)=6,\\
a(6)&=A002110(3)=30,\\
a(7)&=A002110(4)=210,\\
a(10)&=A002110(5)=2310.
\end{aligned}}
\]
